newsitem.title: USA: Can N.Y.C. mayor expect a bigger cash surplus?.
newsitem.headline: Can N.Y.C. mayor expect a bigger cash surplus?.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who has the happy task of divvying up a nearly $1.2 billion surplus, might have an even bigger sum by the end of this fiscal year, a city source said on Friday.
The source, who declined to be named, noted that the mayor's plan includes an extra $146 million in the 1997 fiscal year, which ends on June 30.
The city had collected this extra cash by the end of December, mainly because profits earned by Wall Street banks and brokers continued to outpace forcasts.

The sum, which gets added to the $450 million in extra cash the city announced in November, might rise further if the economy stays strong and if Wall Street banks and brokers, whose profits are highly volatile, do not get slammed by a bear market in the last half of the city's fiscal year.

The source speculated a conservative estimate of the extra cash the city might get could be as high as $150 million. Further, he said that the latest data show that the Board of Education has a nearly $71 million surplus, though it plans to spend the money.
A spokesmen for Giuliani and the Board of Education were not immediately available to comment.
The positive outlook for New York City's revenues was not entirely dismissed by the City of New York Independent Budget Office, which is an independent body.
Douglas Criscitello, director, said: "I'd say it's not unlikely.
"The economy could continue to outperform estimates, it's very possible, who knows the Dow Jones Industrial Average could be up another 1,000 or 2,000 points by the end of the fiscal year," he said.
Bob Kurtter, a vice president at Moody's Investors Service, said that the city probably has captured the vast majority of the unexpected rise in revenues.
But bonuses for Wall Street employees still might trickle in over the next two months, and if equities markets stay robust, capital gains tax collections could rise.
So both New York City and New York State could see revenues firm.
"I think in both cases, it's possible that even with as much as the state and city have realized, there may be even more," Kurtter said.

However, another city source, who declined to be named, said he would be stunned if New York City's revenues rose sharply over the next six months, saying that the timing of personal and corporate taxes made such a scenario unlikely.
"I'm flabbergasted at the number and the dollar for the year," the source said, referring to the $150 million estimate. He added there was no surplus the Board of Education.
One sign of how the city's revenues are shaping up at least for the start of the second half of the city's fiscal year will be available soon, when personal income tax data for January are released.
"We'll have a good indiciation by early next week as to where the city's revenues are going," said Tom McMahon, director of finance, for the City Council.

Fiscal monitors and bond rating agencies praised as prudent the Giuliani Adminstration's decision to use a conservative forecast for fiscal 1997 revenues and noted it is not uncommon for elected officials to err on the side of underestimating, at least in the current year, to avoid the problems that can develop if there are any shortfalls.
While Wall Street firms earned more than $11 billion in 1996, the city is only projecting about $4.7 billion of profits for them, which would be a moderate year for them.

The preliminary budget that the mayor proposed for fiscal 1998 won cautious praise from fiscal monitors and bond rating agencies, though they cited continuing problems with large, out-year gaps, and fretted about potential risks.
City agencies are expected to fight $558 million in cuts that Giuliani proposed, which includes a plan to slice $114 million from the Health and Hospital Corp's budget.
The Democrat-led City Council, in a prepared statement, has said its biggest concerns were healthcare cuts, and also noted the mayor's plan did not offer any more cash for libraries.
Unions, especially one representing police officers, who have not had a contract for nearly two years, also are expected to demand a share of any further surpluses.

Fiscal monitors and rating agencies pointed out the preliminary 1998 budget assumes Albany lawmakers agree on $338 milion of Medicaid savings, which are like ones they rejected in the past, and an additional $210 million in state aid that might not materialize.

They added the Municipal Assistance Corp for the City of New York has yet to agree to provide more than $125 million of the $250 million that Giuliani assumes he will get for educational and other programs.
